title: Line & Contour

learn.summary: A confident wrong line beats a timid right one — hesitant, hairy, scratched-out lines are the universal beginner tell. Drawabox drills exactly this: plan the stroke, then execute it once, fast, without correcting. Contour work meanwhile teaches your eye to crawl along edges at drawing speed.

do: Fill one page today with single-stroke straight lines between pre-marked dot pairs — no corrections allowed — and circle your ten straightest.

children.title: Blind Contour

learn.summary: In blind contour drawing you trace an object's edges with your eyes while your pencil follows — without ever looking at the paper. The results look absurd and that is irrelevant: the exercise welds eye movement to hand movement. Kimon Nicolaides' The Natural Way to Draw made it the opening ritual of art education.

do: Do three 5-minute blind contour drawings of your non-drawing hand this week, never once glancing at the paper mid-drawing.

children.title: Ghosting & Confidence

learn.summary: Drawabox's ghosting method: hover your pen over the intended stroke several times to rehearse the motion, then commit in one smooth, quick pass. Speed produces smoothness because a fast arm can't micro-correct into wobbles. Ink is deliberately used so mistakes cannot be erased — you learn to own the line and move on.

do: Using a pen (no eraser), ghost and execute 50 lines and 30 ellipses today; mark each one as confident or wobbly and count your ratio.

children.title: Drawing from the Shoulder

learn.summary: Wrist-only drawing produces short, cramped, curved strokes; long clean lines come from the shoulder with the wrist locked. This is why ateliers put beginners at easels with paper vertical — it makes shoulder movement the default. Retraining feels awkward for about two weeks and then becomes permanent.

do: Tape a large sheet to a wall and draw 20 long sweeping lines and 20 big circles using only shoulder movement, keeping your wrist completely rigid.

children.title: Line Weight

learn.summary: Varying line thickness creates hierarchy for free: heavier lines advance, sit in shadow, or carry weight; lighter lines recede and describe interior detail. Master draftsmen often thicken the underside of forms and where objects overlap. One drawing redone with deliberate line weight instantly looks a year more skilled.

do: Take one recent line drawing and go back over it, thickening only the outer silhouette and the shadowed undersides — compare before and after photos.

reflect: Compare today's contour drawing with your first one. What does your line do now that it couldn't do then?
